title: Influence of Turn-Taking in a Two-Person Conversation on the Gaze of a Viewer
finding: Eye-tracking of non-involved viewers watching a video of a two-person conversation: viewers' gaze followed, rather than predicted, the change of speaker at turn transitions; visual-only or audio-only versions also shifted gaze to the speaker, but less and later than with both modalities (per authors).
why_for_us: In a two-shot the viewer's eye lands on whoever speaks, slightly late; a held silence where nobody speaks frees the eye to drift to the listener, so a pause is the moment to put Kuba's or Zosia's unspoken reaction on screen.

title: Watching You Watch Movies: Using Eye Tracking to Inform Cognitive Film Theory
finding: Chapter in the edited volume Psychocinematics; the OpenAlex record carries only the book synopsis, which frames the volume as an empirical, cognitive-science approach to how film techniques capture viewers' sensations, thoughts and feelings.
why_for_us: Background reference for why eye-tracking evidence, not intuition, should decide where the glance beat sits in a 9:16 frame; read the chapter itself before citing specifics.

title: Are you seeing what I'm seeing? An eye-tracking evaluation of dynamic scenes
finding: Over 400 exhibition visitors watched scenes from Hitchcock's Vertigo while eye movements were recorded; the paper proposes visualisations and metrics for testing how directorial techniques steer viewers' gaze (per authors; methods paper, no effect sizes in abstract).
why_for_us: Supports testing our cut of a glance-exchange scene with cheap webcam eye tracking before publishing, instead of assuming the audience sees the look.

title: Perceptual psychological approach on Shot/Reverse Shot
finding: Tobii eye-tracking of viewers watching shot/reverse-shot dialogue: the hypothesis that gaze moves from the main character to the other person or into off-screen space was not confirmed; shots were short bust shots and viewers seemed to expect the reverse shot rather than search the frame edge (per author; small, uncited study).
why_for_us: Shot/reverse-shot is a schema viewers anticipate, so an unexpected withheld reverse shot (we stay on Zosia while Kuba is off-screen) is what makes a look register as longing.

title: Glances, glares, and glowering: how should a virtual human express emotion through gaze?
finding: OpenAlex holds no abstract; the record's keywords place it on real-time animation of emotional gaze shifts in virtual humans as a nonverbal channel.
why_for_us: Relevant because our avatars have limited facial range: gaze-shift timing and direction may carry the emotion the face cannot; check the full text for which gaze parameters the authors manipulated.

title: Intimacy is Induced and Regulated Through Proxemic & Gaze Behaviour - A Study in Immersive Virtual Reality
finding: In immersive VR, participants reacted most strongly when agents changed both distance and gaze; more intimate moves (closer, more mutual gaze) triggered gaze aversion and stepping back, less intimate ones (farther, averted gaze) drew more mutual gaze and approach; gaze-only changes had weaker effects than distance-only (per author; master's thesis).
why_for_us: Equilibrium logic for the slow burn: when one character leans in or holds a look, the other should look away or step back, and a look-away invites the partner's look; do not stack closeness and mutual gaze in the same beat too early.

title: Between the Averted Gaze and the Male Gaze: Women in Farhadi’s Films as Tentative Harbingers of Cinematic Islamic Feminism
venue: The International Journal of the Image
finding: Essay reading Asghar Farhadi's female characters through the tension between the averted gaze and the male gaze, as agents caught in patriarchal constraint who imagine escape.
why_for_us: Averted gaze can read as constraint and inner life rather than shyness; useful framing so Zosia's look-away reads as choice and professional restraint, not coyness.

title: Krzysztof Kieslowski’nin “A Short Film About Love” Filminde Bakışın İnşası ve Cinsiyetsizleşmesi
finding: Essay (in Turkish) on how Kieślowski's A Short Film About Love constructs the look and scopophilic pleasure and then de-genders the gaze, against the classical model in which the man watches and the woman is watched.
why_for_us: A Polish reference point for a slow-burn built almost entirely on looking; also a warning that one-sided watching reads as voyeurism, so the glances between Kuba and Zosia should be mutual and consensual.

title: Watching Closely: Shot Scale Influences Theory of Mind Response in Visual Narratives
finding: Within-subject study with four short animated films annotated for average shot scale, plus story retelling and skin conductance: in a Poisson regression, closer average shot scale predicted more mental-state references in viewers' retellings (per authors).
why_for_us: Close shots make viewers read thoughts into a character even when the face does little, which suits avatars with limited expressiveness: put the unsaid feeling in a tight vertical close-up rather than in dialogue.

title: Watching More Closely: Shot Scale Affects Film Viewers’ Theory of Mind Tendency But Not Ability
finding: Between-subject experiment (N=136) with manipulated film scenes: close-ups (vs long shots) raised viewers' tendency to attribute mental states only when the character's face was sad, not neutral; the effect did not spread to other characters or change general Theory of Mind ability (per authors).
why_for_us: A close-up alone does not create feeling: it amplifies an expression that is already there, so the avatar needs at least a small readable expression (a tightened mouth, a lowered gaze) in the close shot.

title: Shot scale matters: The effect of close-up frequency on mental state attribution in film viewers
finding: Online experiment (N=495), 13 versions of an animated film, 6 close-up frequencies x 2 facial expressions plus a zero-close-up control: more close-ups raised spontaneous (not prompted) mental-state attribution up to a point, beyond which it declined (per authors).
why_for_us: Inverted-U for close-ups: in a 60-90 s episode, two or three well-placed close-ups of a glance do more than a whole episode of faces; vary with medium two-shots.

title: On the Influence of Shot Scale on Film Mood and Narrative Engagement in Film Viewers
finding: Shot scale was auto-classified by CNNs trained on 120 films by six directors; distribution and rotation of close, medium and long shots were related to viewers' mood ratings (hedonic tone, energetic and tense arousal) on 50 clips and to narrative engagement for violent scenes (per authors; abstract gives no effect sizes).
why_for_us: Shot-scale rhythm is itself a mood control; a tool like this could audit our AI-generated cuts so a tender beat is not accidentally cut like a tense one.

title: Shaping film: A quantitative formal analysis of contemporary empathy-eliciting Hollywood cinema.
venue: Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts
finding: Formal analysis of 100 empathy-eliciting scenes from contemporary Hollywood films found no single empathic style, but PCA and correlations pointed to general principles: reducing perceived distance through close-ups and face depiction, balancing arousing features with comprehensible visual complexity, and keeping coherence and low visual contrast (per authors).
why_for_us: For intimate beats keep the vertical frame uncluttered, low-contrast and close on faces; busy notary-office backgrounds or flashy AI artefacts work against empathy.

title: Dynamics of Viewer's Attention: Making Content More Engaging in a Vertical Frame
finding: Webcam eye-tracking, within-subjects, N=40, two 20-s vertical (9:16) stimulus videos: a centrally positioned area of interest produced longer fixations, fewer saccades and a higher fixation/saccade ratio than a subject moving around the frame (per authors).
why_for_us: In 9:16 keep the face carrying the glance in the central third; moving it around the frame costs attention. Small sample and weak venue, so treat as a pointer.

title: The Reticent Close-Up
venue: Routledge eBooks (Companion to American Film History)
finding: Chapter on Fox editor Barbara McLean, who pushed directors to shoot more close-ups to gain control over performances; the author argues her films show that continuity editing with close-ups can produce nuanced, understated effects usually credited to the long take.
why_for_us: Understatement can be built in the edit: with limited avatar acting, choose and trim close-ups so restraint comes from cutting, not from a long take the model cannot sustain.

title: A question of proximity: exploring a new screen grammar for 360-degree cinematic virtual reality
finding: Essay arguing that in 360-degree cinematic VR, where there are no close-ups or long shots in the classical sense, Hall's proxemics (intimate, personal, social distance) can serve as a new screen grammar for staging.
why_for_us: Gives a vocabulary to brief the video model by distance between characters (intimate under ~45 cm vs personal vs social) rather than by shot size alone; the slow burn can be tracked as the zone the two apprentices dare to enter.

title: RESTRAINING THE MOOD FOR LOVE: A SEMIOTIC ANALYSIS OF WONG KAR WAI’S IN THE MOOD FOR LOVE
finding: Semiotic essay (Peirce, Barthes) on how cinematography and mise-en-scène in In the Mood for Love carry the theme of restraint through objects, characters' actions and framing.
why_for_us: Restraint can be carried by objects and repeated framings (a corridor, a doorway, the same staircase) rather than by expression, which suits avatars; a recurring notary-office doorway can play this role.

title: Hors-vue, hors-champ, hors-film: In the Mood for Love et l’esthétique de l’occultation
finding: Essay (in French) arguing that beneath its romantic surface In the Mood for Love is radical in image composition and narrative construction, built on an aesthetic of hiding: what is out of view, out of frame and out of the film.
why_for_us: Withholding is a tool: keep key moments off-screen (the reply never shown, a hand just outside the 9:16 edge) and let the narrow vertical frame do the hiding.

title: The Mechanism of Visual Confinement and Affective Accumulation in the Cinematic Viewing Experience: An Analysis of the Film In the Mood for Love
finding: Mise-en-scène essay arguing that In the Mood for Love's force comes less from confession or conflict than from making desire hard to see, approach and complete, through confined space and obstructed views.
why_for_us: Confined, obstructed framing (glass partitions, file cabinets, half-open doors) as the visual form of a love that must not cross into professional territory. Weak venue; the same text appears under another venue as W7213315151.

title: The Sensuous Cinema of Wong Kar-wai: Film Poetics and the Aesthetic of Disturbance, Second Edition
finding: Monograph arguing that Wong's films produce sensuousness and disturbance through narrative disruptions, jarring cuts and the blocking of facial access, which jolt the viewer out of full aesthetic absorption.
why_for_us: Blocking facial access (faces turned away, half-hidden) is a recognised art-cinema device and a practical cover for limited avatar expressiveness.

title: Interruption/Interaction/Collaboration: A Critical Appraisal of the Textual @traction Interactive Event
finding: Filmmaker's reflective essay on a 12-minute 35 mm short in which messages sent to a lost mobile phone let two men declare their love; the film withholds sight of the crucial messages that drive the characters' actions.
why_for_us: Direct precedent for the unsent or unseen message: never show its text, only the typing, the hesitation, the deleting; it also keeps any client data out of frame.

title: Reporting pauses in dramatic dialogue
finding: No abstract in OpenAlex; the record's keywords indicate an experiment on how listeners perceive and estimate pause durations in performed dramatic dialogue (Hamlet), with articulation rate and listener gender.
why_for_us: Relevant to timing AI-voice pauses; check the full text before using any duration figure.

title: The captivating use of silence in film : How silence affects the emotional aspect of cinema
finding: Bachelor-level thesis combining film and literature review, qualitative interviews and the author's own test production to examine whether creative use of sound and silence is needed to evoke emotion.
why_for_us: Weak evidence, but a practical checklist for designing silence (room tone kept, music dropped) instead of dead air from TTS gaps.

title: ... Simply Because You're near Me: Love, Chungking Express and in the Mood for Love
finding: Essay on love in Wong Kar-wai's films, opening with In the Mood for Love's epigraph: she keeps her head lowered to give him a chance to come closer, but he cannot for lack of courage, and she walks away.
why_for_us: Template for an interrupted-meeting beat: one offers a small opening, the other hesitates, the moment passes; that missed chance is the slow-burn engine.

title: Now You’ve Got the Shiveries: Affect, Intimacy, and the ASMR Whisper Community
finding: Cultural analysis of the ASMR whisper community: its videos rely mainly on the affective power of the whispered voice to create an intimate sonic space shared by listener and whisperer, a pleasure the community must defend against perceptions of it as transgressive.
why_for_us: A close-mic, whispered or low voice creates intimacy on headphones, the default for vertical video; but it can tip into sexualised or uncomfortable, so use it for one line, not a whole scene, in an office setting.

title: Sonic intimacy in the music of Billie Eilish and recordings that induce ASMR
finding: Reports the method and preliminary results of a study of emotional responses to Billie Eilish's music, mouth-related ASMR sounds (wetness, whispering, breathing) and non-mouth sounds (tapping, scratching), and proposes a theory of sonic intimacy based on close-mic electroacoustic techniques shared with Bing Crosby (per authors; preliminary).
why_for_us: Breathing and close-mic voice quality are a deliberate intimacy cue; when generating the AI voice, test a breathier, closer take for the inner-voice line of the unsent message.

title: Different Vocal Parameters Predict Perceptions of Dominance and Attractiveness
finding: Using natural speech from an unscripted dating game rather than standardized speech, the authors examined which vocal parameters predict men's voices being judged dominant (by men) and attractive (by women); prior work linked low mean F0 to both, and here different parameters predicted each judgement (per authors; abstract truncated).
why_for_us: Dominance and attractiveness are separate vocal settings; for Kuba's voice aim for warmth and attractiveness without a dominant, authoritative register that would clash with a lateral, peer romance.

title: Towards a More Nuanced View of Vocal Attractiveness
finding: Californian men and women rated the attractiveness of 30 male and 30 female voices reading words; ratings by both sexes were highly correlated, with men rating male voices lower than women did, and acoustic analyses with PCA related vowel and voice-quality measures to ratings (per authors).
why_for_us: Listeners largely agree on which voices are attractive, so a small listening panel is a reasonable way to pick AI voices for Kuba and Zosia.

title: Building Trust Through Voice: How Vocal Tone Impacts User Perception of Attractiveness of Voice Assistants
finding: Experiment showing that the tone of a voice assistant's voice significantly affects its perceived attractiveness and trustworthiness, with participants more drawn to assistants with certain tones (per authors; preprint, abstract truncated).
why_for_us: Tone of a synthetic voice is a controllable lever for warmth and trust; tune it before tuning the script.

title: Can You Hear the Love Tonight? Creating Cinematic Romance with Diegetic Songs
finding: Chapter arguing that romance is an affective experience produced by style as much as narrative, and examining scenes in non-musical films where diegetic popular songs portray and shape romantic love, drawing on research on music listening effects.
why_for_us: A song the characters themselves hear (a radio in the office kitchen, a phone speaker) can mark a shared moment more delicately than a swelling score; mind music licensing.

title: Loving Out Loud: Romantic Coupling in Early Sound Films, 1928–1933
finding: Historical study of the critical reception of love scenes in early Hollywood sound films, asking why they failed and how Hollywood fixed them, and analysing two musical techniques (drifts and jumps) in ballroom love scenes.
why_for_us: Spoken love scenes failed when sound was new; the fix was music and restraint, a lesson for AI voices that can sound flat: say less, let music carry the drift.

title: Parasocial Interactions in Otome Games: Emotional Engagement and Parasocial Intimacy Among Chinese Female Players
finding: Qualitative study of female otome players: parasocial romances are embedded in daily life through game mechanics and players' imagination, offering emotional support, regulation of negative emotions and identity work; only a minority named the lack of physical contact as a shortcoming (per authors).
why_for_us: Audiences can accept romance with non-human, animated partners when emotional responsiveness is high; touch is not required, which suits our touch-free professional slow burn.

title: Simulated Intimacy, but Real Connection: Perceived Reciprocity and Romantic Closeness make Otome Fun to Play
finding: Survey of 293 Chinese otome players supported a model in which perceived reciprocity raises romantic closeness with NPCs, which raises enjoyment and appreciation; players reported high reciprocity and felt the NPCs contributed more than they did (per authors; cross-sectional).
why_for_us: Reciprocity is the engine: each episode should give both apprentices a small, visible gesture back (returning a borrowed pen, waiting for the other), not one-sided pining.

title: Constructing the meaning of human– AI romantic relationships from the perspectives of users dating the social chatbot Replika
finding: Contrapuntal analysis of Replika community posts found two interplaying discourses, idealization and realism, through which users construct and negotiate what an AI partner means; communication is central (per authors; qualitative).
why_for_us: Viewers hold idealization and realism at once; an AI-generated couple can be loved as ideal while the series stays honest about being artificial, so the tone should not pretend otherwise.

title: Fictosexuality, Fictoromance, and Fictophilia: A Qualitative Study of Love and Desire for Fictional Characters
finding: Thematic analysis of 71 online discussions on strong, lasting love or desire for fictional characters found five themes, including the fictophilic paradox, stigma, behaviours and asexuality (per authors).
why_for_us: Strong attachment to fictional characters is real and sometimes stigmatised; community management should treat fans' crushes on Kuba or Zosia respectfully.

title: Perceptual effects of damped and exaggerated facial motion in animated characters
finding: Cartoon and realistic-looking characters were animated with tracked actor motion exaggerated or damped in 10% steps up to 40%; changes of about plus or minus 20% shifted likeability and intelligence ratings differently: realistic characters benefited from more motion, cartoon characters from damped motion; facial motion correlated with perceived extraversion (per authors).
why_for_us: For realistic-looking AI avatars, slightly amplifying facial motion helps rather than hurts, while stylised ones read better damped; choose the avatar style first, then tune expression intensity in the matching direction.

title: Raise Your Eyebrows Higher: Facilitating Emotional Communication in Social Virtual Reality Through Region-Specific Facial Expression Exaggeration
finding: Study 1 (N=30): exaggerating avatar expressions lowered realism for joy, surprise and disgust (overly dramatic mouths) but raised it for fear, sadness and anger (upper-face emotions); Study 2 (N=20): exaggerating only the upper face raised emotional intensity and contagion for negative emotions while reducing uncanny effects (per authors).
why_for_us: Region-specific rule for our avatars: push eyebrows and eyes slightly, keep the mouth natural; longing and hesitation live in the upper face.

title: Effect of avatar stylization and facial expression intensity in virtual interactions
finding: VR study (N=40) with an actress-driven avatar at three stylization levels and three expression-intensity levels: co-presence was higher with the stylized than the realistic avatar regardless of intensity; stylized and semi-realistic avatars scored better on eeriness and trust; augmenting expressions had no negative effect (per authors).
why_for_us: Semi-realistic or stylized avatars may feel warmer and less eerie than photoreal ones; stronger expressions did not backfire here.

title: Effect of Appearance and Animation Realism on the Perception of Emotionally Expressive Virtual Humans
finding: User experiment varying appearance realism and animation realism of an emotionally expressive virtual human: higher appearance and animation realism raised social presence and attractiveness ratings, and animation realism affected perceived realism and emotion intensity (per authors).
why_for_us: Animation quality matters more than looks for emotional read; spend generation budget on natural micro-motion in the glance shots.

title: When Digital Human Avatars Emote, Users Pull Back: The Hidden Cost of Expressiveness in Trust and App Engagement
finding: Three experiments (health and tourism apps): emotional expressiveness of digital human avatars lowered intention to use the app, mediated by lower trust, with the indirect effect holding for people low in anthropomorphism tendency (per authors).
why_for_us: Open display of emotion by a digital human can reduce trust; for AI avatars understated emotion is not only a style choice but may protect credibility.

title: Attraction in organizations: A model of workplace romance
finding: Theoretical review proposing antecedents and consequences of workplace romance, derived from social-psychological theories of interpersonal and romantic attraction, love, emotion and social exchange plus earlier workplace-romance research.
why_for_us: Proximity, repeated exposure and shared work are the classic antecedents; apprentices from two offices meeting on joint transactions is a realistic setup.

title: Workplace Romances between Senior- Level Executives and Lower-Level Employees: An Issue of Work Disruption and Gender
finding: Vignette experiment (2x2, part-time MBA students): respondents attributed a job motive more to a female than a male lower-level partner in a hierarchical romance; perceived job motive raised perceived organizational harm and preference for management action, and men would act more strongly as co-workers (per author).
why_for_us: Hierarchical romance triggers suspicion of career motives and gendered blame; keeping Kuba and Zosia as equal-rank apprentices from different offices avoids this trap.

title: When Work and Love Mix: Perceptions of Peers in Workplace Romances
finding: Full-time employees in a 2 (peer sex) x 2 (partner status) design reported less solidarity and trust and more information manipulation towards a peer dating a superior than a peer dating another peer; trust mediated these effects (per authors).
why_for_us: Lateral peer romance is judged far more leniently than romance with a boss, supporting the apprentice-apprentice premise; colleagues' trust is the stake to dramatise.

title: Mixing Pleasure with Work: Employee Perceptions of and Responses to Workplace Romance
finding: 2x4 experiment with 212 working adults judging a hypothetical coworker dating a peer, superior, subordinate or outsider: peers dating superiors were seen as more job-motivated, less love-motivated and more likely to get unfair advantages (per authors; abstract truncated).
why_for_us: Dating someone outside one's own organisation (our two offices) is one of the conditions tested; the dramatic risk is not colleagues' jealousy but perceived conflict of interest between the two offices.

title: Love at the Office? Understanding Workplace Romance Disclosures and Reactions from the Coworker Perspective
finding: Qualitative study of how coworkers learn about workplace romances and react; it identified two themes about disclosure and subsequent reactions (per authors; abstract truncated).
why_for_us: How colleagues find out (a noticed glance, a slip) is a ready-made episode hook; read the themes before scripting the office-gossip arc.

title: Workplace Romance and Career Reputation Effects across Industries
finding: Internet survey of close to 1,000 adults in major US cities: beliefs about career-reputation effects, occurrence and comfort with workplace romance differed by industry (Healthcare, Education, Administration and Other Professional most conservative), interacted with sex, management status and age, and romances were seen as more damaging to women's careers (per authors).
why_for_us: Professional services are a conservative setting, so caution and secrecy are realistic; the cost would fall harder on Zosia, a tension the script can acknowledge.

title: Romantic Relationships at Work: Why Love Can Hurt
finding: Literature review arguing that power is key to understanding the negative consequences of workplace romance for individuals and organizations, covering definitions, prevalence and types (per author).
why_for_us: Power asymmetry is what turns romance into harm; keep supervisors (the notaries) out of the romance and show the apprentices aware of it.

title: Don't Screw the Crew: Exploring the Rules of Engagement in Organizational Romance
finding: Qualitative study drawing on the sexuality-of-organization literature to explore participants' own informal rules of engagement for organizational romance, as opposed to survey and policy-focused management research (per authors; abstract truncated).
why_for_us: Informal rules (do not date your own team) suggest why a romance across two offices is the 'acceptable' one, and what unwritten rules the characters would cite.

title: Dating Among the Profession: Ethical Guidance in the Area of Personal Dating Conflicts of Interest
finding: Law-review article with no abstract in OpenAlex; its title and keywords place it on ethical guidance for conflicts of interest arising when lawyers date other members of the profession.
why_for_us: The closest match to Kuba and Zosia: two professionals from different offices dating creates conflict-of-interest questions; read it for the disclosure and withdrawal logic the plot should respect.

title: Sexual and nonsexual boundaries in professional relationships: principles and teaching guidelines
finding: Teaching paper: healthy professional relationships require boundaries, especially with a power differential; violations are grouped as sexual harassment, sexual misconduct or exploitation, and nonsexual dual relationships (per author).
why_for_us: A clear taxonomy for what the series must never show: no exploitation of clients or juniors, and no dual roles where a character advises a matter involving the partner.

title: Bad Lawyers in the Movies
finding: No abstract in OpenAlex; an essay by a law-and-film scholar on the portrayal of unethical lawyers in film.
why_for_us: Reference for the cliché the series must avoid (the lawyer who breaks rules for love) and for why audiences expect it.

title: Defending the Guilty: Lawyer Ethics in the Movies
finding: Essay on how films portray lawyers' ethical duties to clients, opening with Atticus Finch in To Kill a Mockingbird as the model of discharging that duty.
why_for_us: Films judge lawyers by loyalty to clients; our characters earn sympathy by protecting client secrets even at personal cost.

title: Lawyers, Clients and Assurances of Confidentiality: Lawyers Talking without Speaking, Clients Hearing Without Listening
finding: Essay arguing that new clients approach interviews anxious, that confidentiality doctrines aim to foster candour but clients rarely understand confidentiality without explanation, and that attorneys are ethically obliged to explain it, though typical explanations fall short (per author).
why_for_us: A scene where an apprentice explains secrecy to a nervous client shows professionalism and gives the romance a boundary: what they cannot tell each other.

title: Gemeenschappelijke normen voor vertrouwensberoepen: Tuchtrechtelijke uitspraken over de tuchtnormen voor accountants, advocaten en artsen
finding: Dutch doctoral thesis comparing disciplinary rulings for three 'trusted professions' (accountants, lawyers, doctors), arguing they share defining characteristics and common disciplinary norms (per author).
why_for_us: Supports treating notarial secrecy as part of a shared European trusted-profession ethic; useful for an on-screen line on why a notary's apprentice cannot share files, even with a partner.

title: Framing Female Lawyers: Women on Trial in Film
finding: Book arguing that Reagan-Bush era Hollywood films with women lawyers as protagonists reveal contradictions and anxieties beneath their apparent acceptance of women's professional roles.
why_for_us: Warns against a script that punishes the professional woman for her romance; Zosia's competence should not be undermined by the love plot.
